notes.front: What are the four OpenGitOps principles?
notes.back:
1. Declarative – desired state is expressed declaratively.
2. Versioned and immutable – stored with full history.
3. Pulled automatically – agents pull desired state from the source.
4. Continuously reconciled – agents observe actual state and converge it.

notes.front: Push-based vs pull-based deployment: core difference and security implication?
notes.back:
Push: Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline holds cluster credentials and applies changes.
Pull: an in-cluster agent pulls from Git/OCI. Cluster credentials never leave the cluster; only read access to the source is needed. Pull also gives continuous drift correction.

notes.front: Why is Git (or an OCI registry) alone not sufficient to call a setup 'GitOps'?
notes.back: Without continuous reconciliation, drift from manual changes is never detected or corrected. A one-shot kubectl apply from CI is push-based CD, not GitOps.

notes.front: Common patterns to manage secrets in GitOps repos?
notes.back:
Encrypted-in-Git: Sealed Secrets, Secrets OPerationS (SOPS).
Reference-in-Git: External Secrets Operator (ESO), Secrets Store CSI driver – Git holds only a pointer to Vault / cloud Key Management Service (KMS).

notes.front: Environment promotion: branch-per-environment vs directory-per-environment?
notes.back: Directory (or overlay) per environment on one branch is generally preferred: diffs between envs are visible, no cherry-pick/merge drift between long-lived branches. Branch-per-env tends to diverge.

notes.front: Declarative vs imperative Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
notes.back:
Declarative: describe the end state (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests); the tool computes the diff.
Imperative: describe the steps (shell scripts, many Ansible playbooks, SDK scripts).

notes.front: What does idempotency mean in IaC and why does it matter?
notes.back: Applying the same configuration N times yields the same result as applying it once. Enables safe retries, re-runs and continuous reconciliation.

notes.front: What is configuration drift?
notes.back: Divergence between the declared state and the real infrastructure, typically from manual/out-of-band changes. Detected by terraform plan (refresh) or continuously by reconcilers (Crossplane, Argo CD, Flux).

notes.front: Mutable vs immutable infrastructure?
notes.back:
Mutable: servers are patched/changed in place → snowflakes, drift.
Immutable: never modify; build a new artifact/image and replace instances. Easier rollback, reproducibility.

notes.front: What is Terraform state and why is it needed?
notes.back: A mapping of config resource addresses → real-world object IDs plus cached attributes and dependency metadata. Needed to know what Terraform manages, compute diffs, and order destroys.

notes.front: Why must remote Terraform state be locked, and how is it typically done?
notes.back:
To prevent concurrent applies corrupting state / racing changes.
S3 backend: native lockfile (use_lockfile = true, Terraform ≥1.10) or legacy DynamoDB table; azurerm: blob lease; gcs: lock object; HCP Terraform: built-in.

notes.front: Security concern with Terraform state?
notes.back: State stores attribute values in plaintext, including secrets (DB passwords, keys) even when marked sensitive. Encrypt the backend at rest, restrict access. OpenTofu offers client-side state encryption.

notes.front: count vs for_each: why prefer for_each for collections?
notes.back: count addresses by index (res[0]); removing a middle element shifts indices → destroys/recreates. for_each addresses by stable key (res["web"]).

notes.front: Name the four lifecycle meta-arguments and their purpose.
notes.back:
create_before_destroy – avoid downtime on replacement.
prevent_destroy – error on any plan that destroys it.
ignore_changes – ignore drift on listed attributes.
replace_triggered_by – force replace when referenced item changes.
(Also precondition/postcondition blocks.)

notes.front: How do you rename/move a resource in Terraform without destroying it?
notes.back: A moved { from = ... to = ... } block (Terraform ≥1.1), or legacy terraform state mv. moved is declarative and reviewable in a pull request.

notes.front: How do you bring an existing resource under Terraform management?
notes.back: import { to = aws_s3_bucket.b id = "name" } block (≥1.5), optionally with terraform plan -generate-config-out=gen.tf; or legacy CLI terraform import.

notes.front: Why is terraform apply -target considered dangerous?
notes.back: Applies a partial graph: leaves state inconsistent with config and skips dependent changes. Intended only for exceptional recovery, not routine use.

notes.front: Purpose of .terraform.lock.hcl?
notes.back: Dependency lock file: pins exact provider versions and checksums for reproducible init. Commit it. (Does not lock module versions.)

notes.front: Resource vs data source vs module vs provider?
notes.back:
Resource: object Terraform manages (create/update/delete).
Data source: read-only lookup.
Module: reusable container of resources with inputs/outputs.
Provider: plugin talking to an API.

notes.front: When do you need explicit depends_on?
notes.back: Only for hidden dependencies not expressed via references (e.g. an IAM policy that must exist before an app uses it). Overuse makes plans less precise.

notes.front: What is terraform plan -refresh-only for?
notes.back: Shows/accepts drift: updates state to match reality without proposing infrastructure changes. Replaces deprecated terraform refresh.

notes.front: Terraform CLI workspaces: what are they and their caveat?
notes.back: Multiple state files for the same configuration (terraform.workspace). Same backend & credentials for all, so weak isolation; many teams prefer separate root modules/directories per environment.

notes.front: What is OpenTofu and why does it exist?
notes.back: Open-source fork of Terraform under the Linux Foundation, created after HashiCorp moved Terraform to the Business Source License (BSL) in August 2023. Largely drop-in compatible; adds e.g. state encryption.

notes.front: Pulumi vs Terraform in one line?
notes.back: Same desired-state engine idea, but infrastructure is defined in general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, Go, ...) instead of HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL).

notes.front: What is Crossplane and how does it differ from Terraform?
notes.back: A Kubernetes-native control plane: cloud resources are Custom Resources (CRs) reconciled continuously by providers. Composite Resource Definitions (XRDs) + Compositions build platform APIs. No state file; etcd is the state; drift is auto-corrected.

notes.front: Provisioning vs configuration management?
notes.back: Provisioning creates infrastructure (Terraform, CloudFormation). Configuration management configures what runs on it (Ansible, Puppet, Chef). Ansible is agentless and push-based over SSH.

notes.front: Name policy-as-code tools for IaC.
notes.back: Open Policy Agent (OPA) / Conftest (Rego), HashiCorp Sentinel, Checkov, tfsec/Trivy, Kyverno (Kubernetes).

notes.front: Define chart, release, revision, repository.
notes.back:
Chart: package of templates + defaults.
Release: an installed instance of a chart in a namespace.
Revision: numbered version of a release, incremented by each upgrade/rollback.
Repository: where charts are published (HTTP index or OCI registry).

notes.front: Biggest architectural change from Helm 2 to Helm 3?
notes.back: Removal of Tiller (in-cluster server). Helm 3 is client-only and uses the user's kubeconfig Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Also 3-way merge, release names scoped per namespace, apiVersion: v2 charts.

notes.front: Where does Helm 3 store release information?
notes.back: As Secrets (default driver) in the release's namespace, type helm.sh/release.v1, named sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>. Contains gzipped/base64 manifest, values, chart.

notes.front: Helm values precedence (lowest → highest)?
notes.back: Chart values.yaml → parent chart values for subcharts → -f/--values files (left to right, last wins) → --set / --set-string / --set-file.

notes.front: Explain Helm 3's three-way strategic merge on upgrade.
notes.back: Compares old manifest, live state, and new manifest. Changes made manually in the cluster that conflict with the new chart are overwritten, while unrelated live fields (e.g. sidecars injected) are preserved.

notes.front: include vs template?
notes.back: Both render a named template (define). include returns a string so it can be piped ({{ include "x" . | nindent 4 }}); template is an action and can't be piped.

notes.front: What goes in _helpers.tpl?
notes.back: Named templates (define) like fullname, labels, selectorLabels. Files starting with _ are not rendered as manifests.

notes.front: How does Helm handle CRDs in the crds/ directory?
notes.back: Installed on first install only, never templated, never upgraded, never deleted. Upgrading CRDs must be done out of band (or by shipping them as templates / separate chart).

notes.front: List common Helm hook types and related annotations.
notes.back:
pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade, pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test.
Annotations: helm.sh/hook, helm.sh/hook-weight (ordering), helm.sh/hook-delete-policy (before-hook-creation, hook-succeeded, hook-failed). Hook resources are not part of the release's managed resources.

notes.front: How do you force pods to roll when a ConfigMap rendered by the same chart changes?
notes.back:
Checksum annotation on the pod template:
checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}

notes.front: What does helm upgrade --install --atomic --wait do?
notes.back: Installs if release absent, else upgrades; waits for resources to become ready; on failure automatically rolls back (--atomic implies --wait).

notes.front: Does helm rollback restore an old revision number?
notes.back: No. It creates a new revision whose content equals the target revision.

notes.front: How are chart dependencies declared and fetched?
notes.back: dependencies: in Chart.yaml (name, version, repository, condition, tags, alias). helm dependency update fetches into charts/ and writes Chart.lock.

notes.front: How do parent and subchart share values?
notes.back: Parent sets subchart values under the subchart's name key. .Values.global is visible to parent and all subcharts.

notes.front: What is a library chart?
notes.back: type: library in Chart.yaml. Provides only named templates for reuse; cannot be installed on its own.

notes.front: How do you validate chart values?
notes.back: values.schema.json (JSON Schema) – checked on install/upgrade/lint/template. In templates: required and fail.

notes.front: Pitfall of the lookup function?
notes.back: It queries the live cluster; during helm template or client-side dry-run it returns an empty map. Also empty in Argo CD, which renders via helm template.

notes.front: What does tpl do?
notes.back: Renders a string as a template, e.g. allowing templated values: {{ tpl .Values.host . }}.

notes.front: How do you keep a resource when the release is uninstalled?
notes.back: Annotation helm.sh/resource-policy: keep (commonly on PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) or Secrets). Resource becomes orphaned.

notes.front: helm template vs helm install --dry-run?
notes.back: template: renders locally, no cluster access (no lookup, uses default capabilities). install --dry-run: talks to the cluster for validation/capabilities but does not persist. --dry-run=server enables lookup.

notes.front: How are charts distributed via OCI registries?
notes.back: helm push chart.tgz oci://registry/ns, helm install x oci://registry/ns/chart --version 1.2.3. General Availability (GA) since Helm 3.8. No helm repo add needed.

notes.front: What controls how many release revisions Helm keeps?
notes.back: helm upgrade --history-max (default 10). Older release Secrets are pruned.

notes.front: Notable changes in Helm 4?
notes.back: Released November 2025: server-side apply support, a new WebAssembly-based plugin system, and modernised SDK/logging; Helm 3 charts (apiVersion: v2) remain compatible.

notes.front: What is a Kubernetes Operator?
notes.back: A custom controller paired with Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) that encodes human operational knowledge (install, upgrade, backup, failover) for a specific application into a reconciliation loop.

notes.front: Level-triggered vs edge-triggered and which do controllers use?
notes.back: Edge: react to individual events. Level: act on the current observed state vs desired state. Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered: a missed event is fine because the next reconcile sees full state.

notes.front: Why must Reconcile() be idempotent?
notes.back: It can be called any number of times for the same object (resyncs, requeues, multiple events coalesced). It must converge to the same result without side-effect duplication.

notes.front: spec vs status, and the status subresource?
notes.back: spec = desired state (user-owned); status = observed state (controller-owned). With the /status subresource, status updates go through a separate endpoint and spec updates ignore status, enabling separate RBAC.

notes.front: metadata.generation vs resourceVersion?
notes.back:
generation: increments only on spec changes (with status subresource).
resourceVersion: opaque, changes on any write; used for optimistic concurrency and watches.

notes.front: What is status.observedGeneration for?
notes.back: Controller writes the generation it last reconciled, so clients can tell if status reflects the latest spec.

notes.front: What are finalizers and when does an Operator use them?
notes.back: Strings in metadata.finalizers that block deletion. Deletion sets deletionTimestamp; controller does external cleanup (e.g. delete cloud DB), then removes its finalizer so the object is deleted.

notes.front: How do OwnerReferences work?
notes.back: Child objects point to their owner (controller: true for the managing controller). The garbage collector deletes dependents when the owner is deleted. Must be same namespace (or owner cluster-scoped). Cross-namespace/external → finalizers.

notes.front: Cascading deletion modes?
notes.back:
Background (default): owner deleted immediately, GC deletes dependents.
Foreground: dependents deleted first (foregroundDeletion finalizer).
Orphan: dependents kept, ownerRefs removed.

notes.front: Role of informers, cache and workqueue in client-go/controller-runtime?
notes.back:
Informer: list+watch, keeps a local indexed cache (reads hit the cache, not the API server).
Event handlers enqueue object keys (namespace/name) into a rate-limited, deduplicating workqueue; workers call Reconcile.

notes.front: Why does a controller receive only a namespace/name, not the object diff?
notes.back: Level-triggered design: reconcile reads current state from the cache; events are coalesced by key.

notes.front: Return values of a controller-runtime Reconcile and their effect?
notes.back:
Result{}, nil: done.
Result{RequeueAfter: d}, nil: requeue after d.
_, err: requeue with exponential backoff (rate limiter).

notes.front: How do multiple Operator replicas avoid conflicting?
notes.back: Leader election using a coordination.k8s.io Lease; only the leader runs controllers.

notes.front: How do you handle a 409 Conflict on update?
notes.back: Optimistic concurrency via resourceVersion – re-fetch and retry (retry.RetryOnConflict), or use server-side apply / patches to avoid full-object updates.

notes.front: What is Server-Side Apply (SSA) and why is it useful in controllers?
notes.back: API server merges declared fields and tracks ownership per field manager (managedFields). Controllers send only fields they care about; conflicts are explicit.

notes.front: CRD versioning: served vs storage version, and conversion?
notes.back: Multiple versions can be served; exactly one is storage. Non-trivial schema differences need a conversion webhook (hub-and-spoke conversion in Kubebuilder).

notes.front: Options for validating Custom Resources?
notes.back: OpenAPI v3 schema in the CRD; Common Expression Language (CEL) rules via x-kubernetes-validations (GA 1.29); ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (GA 1.30); validating/mutating admission webhooks.

notes.front: Kubebuilder vs Operator SDK vs controller-runtime?
notes.back:
controller-runtime: Go library (manager, client, cache, reconcilers).
Kubebuilder: scaffolding + controller-gen on top of it.
Operator SDK: builds on Kubebuilder, adds Ansible/Helm operators, Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) bundle and scorecard tooling.

notes.front: Operator Framework capability levels (1–5)?
notes.back: 1 Basic Install, 2 Seamless Upgrades, 3 Full Lifecycle (backup/restore, failure recovery), 4 Deep Insights (metrics, alerts), 5 Auto Pilot (auto-scaling, tuning, healing).

notes.front: What is the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM)?
notes.back: Manages installation, upgrades, dependencies and RBAC of Operators via CatalogSources, Subscriptions, InstallPlans and ClusterServiceVersions (CSVs). Default on OpenShift.

notes.front: Conventional structure of a status condition?
notes.back: type, status (True/False/Unknown), reason (CamelCase), message, lastTransitionTime, observedGeneration. Use meta.SetStatusCondition.

notes.front: How does a controller watch resources it creates and other related objects?
notes.back: For(&MyCR{}) primary; Owns(&appsv1.Deployment{}) enqueues the owner; Watches(src, handler.EnqueueRequestsFromMapFunc(...)) for arbitrary mappings.

notes.front: Purpose of GenerationChangedPredicate?
notes.back: Filters update events so reconcile runs only on spec changes, not on status/metadata-only updates (prevents self-trigger loops).

notes.front: Why avoid writing status on every reconcile unconditionally?
notes.back: Each write changes resourceVersion → triggers another event → hot loop, API server load. Compare before writing.

notes.front: Main Argo CD components?
notes.back: argocd-server (API/UI), argocd-repo-server (clones repos, renders manifests: Helm/Kustomize/plain/plugins), argocd-application-controller (compares live vs desired, syncs), Redis (cache), Dex (Single Sign-On (SSO)), ApplicationSet controller, notifications controller.

notes.front: Key fields of an Application?
notes.back: project, source/sources (repoURL, targetRevision, path/chart, helm/kustomize options), destination (server/name + namespace), syncPolicy.

notes.front: What does an AppProject restrict?
notes.back: Allowed source repos, destination clusters/namespaces, allowed/denied cluster-scoped and namespaced kinds, project roles + JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), sync windows, orphaned resource monitoring.

notes.front: Sync status vs health status?
notes.back:
Sync: does live state match Git (Synced/OutOfSync).
Health: is the app working (Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Suspended, Missing, Unknown) – from built-in or custom Lua health checks.

notes.front: Automated sync options prune and selfHeal?
notes.back:
prune: true – delete resources removed from Git.
selfHeal: true – revert manual live changes (drift) without a new commit. Both off by default even with automated sync.

notes.front: Sync phases and waves?
notes.back: Phases: PreSync → Sync → PostSync (SyncFail on failure). Within a phase, argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave orders resources (lower first, can be negative); Argo waits for health between waves.

notes.front: How are Argo CD hooks declared?
notes.back: argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync|Sync|PostSync|SyncFail|Skip and argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded|HookFailed|BeforeHookCreation. Helm hooks are mapped to these.

notes.front: Is a Helm chart deployed by Argo CD a Helm release?
notes.back: No. Argo renders with helm template and applies manifests itself. helm ls shows nothing; lookup returns empty; lifecycle is Argo's.

notes.front: What is the App of Apps pattern?
notes.back: A parent Application whose source contains Application manifests, bootstrapping a set of child apps from one entry point.

notes.front: ApplicationSet generators?
notes.back: List, Cluster (from registered cluster Secrets/labels), Git (directories or files), Matrix, Merge, SCM Provider, Pull Request, Cluster Decision Resource, Plugin.

notes.front: Typical ApplicationSet for 'deploy addons to every cluster labelled env=prod'?
notes.back: Cluster generator with selector.matchLabels: {env: prod}, templating {{name}}/{{server}} into the Application; often Matrix'd with a Git directory generator.

notes.front: How do multi-source Applications help with Helm?
notes.back: spec.sources lets a chart from a Helm/OCI repo use values files from a separate Git repo via a ref source: valueFiles: [$values/envs/prod.yaml].

notes.front: How do you stop Argo flagging fields mutated by other controllers (e.g. HPA replicas)?
notes.back: ignoreDifferences (jsonPointers/jqPathExpressions/managedFieldsManagers), plus sync option RespectIgnoreDifferences=true so sync doesn't overwrite them.

notes.front: Useful sync options?
notes.back: CreateNamespace=true, ServerSideApply=true, PruneLast=true, ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true, Replace=true, Prune=false (per resource), FailOnSharedResource=true.

notes.front: How does Argo CD track which resources belong to an app?
notes.back: Resource tracking method: annotation (argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id; default since Argo CD 3.0), label (app.kubernetes.io/instance; old default, clashes with Helm labels), or annotation+label.

notes.front: How is a remote cluster registered and stored?
notes.back: argocd cluster add creates a ServiceAccount + RBAC in the target and stores credentials as a Secret labelled argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster in the Argo namespace (can be declared directly).

notes.front: Hub-and-spoke vs instance-per-cluster Argo CD trade-offs?
notes.back:
Hub: single pane of glass, central RBAC, but needs network access + credentials to all clusters and is a blast-radius/scale bottleneck.
Per-cluster: isolation and pull-only networking, but N instances to manage.

notes.front: How often does Argo CD poll Git, and how to speed it up?
notes.back: Default ~3 minutes (timeout.reconciliation, 180s, plus jitter). Configure Git provider webhooks to /api/webhook for immediate refresh.

notes.front: Refresh vs hard refresh?
notes.back:
Refresh: re-compare using cached manifests (checks Git revision).
Hard refresh: invalidate repo-server manifest cache and re-render.

notes.front: How to scale the application controller for many clusters?
notes.back: Run multiple replicas with sharding (by cluster; algorithms legacy / round-robin / consistent-hashing), tune --status-processors and --operation-processors.

notes.front: What are Config Management Plugins (CMPs)?
notes.back: Custom manifest generators run as sidecars on the repo-server (configured via plugin.yaml ConfigManagementPlugin), e.g. for cdk8s, Jsonnet variants, envsubst.

notes.front: Where is Argo CD RBAC configured?
notes.back: argocd-rbac-cm policy.csv (Casbin): p, role:x, applications, sync, proj/*, allow and g, sso-group, role:x; plus AppProject roles.

notes.front: Why do the Argo CD docs discourage manifest-injecting secret plugins (e.g. argocd-vault-plugin)?
notes.back: Secrets end up in rendered manifests cached in Redis/repo-server and visible to anyone who can view the app's manifests. Prefer operators that create Secrets in-cluster (External Secrets, Sealed Secrets).

notes.front: What is Argo Rollouts?
notes.back: Separate controller providing Rollout CRD for blue-green and canary with traffic shaping (Istio, NGINX, Gateway API, ...) and automated analysis (AnalysisTemplates against Prometheus etc.).

notes.front: Flux (GitOps Toolkit) controllers and their roles?
notes.back: source-controller (fetch Git/OCI/Helm/Bucket → artifacts), kustomize-controller (apply Kustomizations), helm-controller (HelmReleases), notification-controller (alerts + inbound webhooks), image-reflector-controller + image-automation-controller (image update automation).

notes.front: Flux source kinds?
notes.back: GitRepository, OCIRepository, HelmRepository (HTTP or OCI type), HelmChart, Bucket (S3-compatible).

notes.front: Flux Kustomization vs Kustomize's kustomization.yaml?
notes.back: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/Kustomization is a CR telling kustomize-controller what path from which source to build/apply, with interval, prune, health checks. kustomize.config.k8s.io/Kustomization is the Kustomize build config file. If absent in the path, Flux generates one.

notes.front: Does a Flux HelmRelease create a real Helm release?
notes.back: Yes. helm-controller uses the Helm SDK; release appears in helm ls, hooks run natively, lookup works.

notes.front: HelmRelease remediation and drift detection?
notes.back:
install.remediation.retries, upgrade.remediation.retries + strategy: rollback|uninstall.
driftDetection.mode: enabled|warn compares live cluster to release manifest and corrects it.

notes.front: How do you order Flux reconciliations?
notes.back: spec.dependsOn on Kustomizations/HelmReleases (e.g. CRDs/infra before apps), combined with wait: true or healthChecks.

notes.front: Meaning of interval, retryInterval, timeout, prune, wait on a Kustomization?
notes.back: interval: reconcile period; retryInterval: retry after failure; timeout: for apply + health; prune: garbage-collect removed objects; wait: wait for all applied resources to be ready.

notes.front: How does Flux decrypt SOPS-encrypted secrets?
notes.back: Natively in kustomize-controller: spec.decryption: {provider: sops, secretRef: {name: sops-age}} (age/PGP keys) or cloud KMS via workload identity.

notes.front: What are post-build variable substitutions?
notes.back: spec.postBuild.substitute and substituteFrom (ConfigMaps/Secrets) replace ${VAR} / ${VAR:=default} after kustomize build. Disable per object with kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/substitute: disabled.

notes.front: What does flux bootstrap do?
notes.back: Installs Flux controllers, commits their manifests plus a GitRepository + Kustomization (flux-system) to the repo, and configures deploy keys – so Flux manages its own installation from Git.

notes.front: How does Flux enforce multi-tenancy?
notes.back: spec.serviceAccountName impersonation per Kustomization/HelmRelease, controller flags --no-cross-namespace-refs and --default-service-account, and spec.targetNamespace.

notes.front: How can Flux deploy to a remote cluster?
notes.back: spec.kubeConfig.secretRef on Kustomization/HelmRelease (or configMapRef for workload-identity based auth) – a hub cluster applies to spoke clusters.

notes.front: Flux image update automation objects?
notes.back: ImageRepository (scan registry tags), ImagePolicy (semver/alphabetical/numerical selection), ImageUpdateAutomation (commit back to Git). Manifests are marked with # {"$imagepolicy": "ns:policy"}.

notes.front: Flux notification objects?
notes.back: Provider (Slack, Teams, GitHub commit status, ...), Alert (which events to which provider), Receiver (inbound webhook that triggers reconcile).

notes.front: How to force or pause a Flux reconciliation?
notes.back: flux reconcile kustomization x --with-source (sets reconcile.fluxcd.io/requestedAt); flux suspend/resume or spec.suspend: true.

notes.front: How does Flux verify artifact authenticity?
notes.back: spec.verify on GitRepository (OpenPGP commit signatures) and OCIRepository (cosign / Notation signatures), e.g. artifacts pushed with flux push artifact.

notes.front: Flux equivalent of Argo Rollouts?
notes.back: Flagger: progressive delivery (canary, A/B, blue-green) with service mesh / ingress traffic shifting and metric analysis.

notes.front: Argo CD vs Flux: key differences?
notes.back:
Argo: built-in UI, Application-centric, Helm via helm template, natural hub-and-spoke, SSO/RBAC in-tool.
Flux: set of composable controllers, no built-in UI, native Helm releases, Kubernetes RBAC + impersonation for tenancy, typically per-cluster pull, strong OCI artifact support.
